title: Your Mini GameDay
scenario: Your team owns the lamp shop and is preparing a release. The team lead asks: “If one of our providers becomes slow or unavailable, can customers still get useful information?” You have time to test one concrete failure in this local Docker shop and recommend a response.
why: The earlier challenges gave you an incident and a path to follow. Now you turn a customer risk into your own repeatable experiment that a teammate could run from your notes.
reproduce: Choose one dependency and one fault: an Inventory or Shipping response delay, or a disconnection. Choose the customer action you want to protect. For example, investigate slow Shipping replies during “Order preview”; record your chosen delay before applying it.
ready: Clear old faults and restore default settings. Use only the two local dependency paths and keep the supplied light traffic. Choose one fault, not a combination, so you can explain what caused the result.
assignment: Design and run one test that answers a specific customer-facing reliability question, then recommend a mitigation with evidence.

tasks.title: Write a customer question and a test plan
tasks.instruction: Name the Storefront button/API route, the dependency, the exact fault and magnitude, and the metric you will watch. Predict the customer effect. State an abort condition: a specific unexpected result that means you will remove the fault immediately.

tasks.title: Measure normal behavior
tasks.instruction: Run the chosen customer action and record a healthy baseline. Choose a consistent observation window, for example 60–90 seconds, for every phase. Keep the supplied traffic unchanged.

tasks.title: Run your chosen failure
tasks.instruction: Use Network Faults to apply only the planned delay or disconnection. Repeat the customer action and record timings, route/status outcomes, and the relevant dependency signals. Decide whether your original prediction matched the evidence.

tasks.title: Make a justified change
tasks.instruction: Remove the fault first. Choose and apply a timeout/fallback change in the Fallbacks & timeouts tab. You can complete this experiment entirely in the browser. Explain what customer behavior it protects and what information or certainty may be lost.

tasks.title: Repeat the exact test and recommend a response
tasks.instruction: Apply the same fault to the same dependency at the same magnitude. Repeat the action and compare equivalent windows. State whether your change helped, document its trade-off and exact reproduction steps, then remove the fault, undo the mitigation, verify recovery, and submit your record.

done: A teammate can reproduce your chosen customer action, fault, mitigation, and rollback from the submitted record.
Your recommendation compares healthy, faulted, and mitigated results under the identical fault.
You explained the remaining risk and restored the clean system.
solution: There is no single correct experiment. A valid record has a baseline, written hypothesis, limited fault, abort condition, measured outcome, mitigation, identical retest, and rollback.

Worked example: test /api/product with +1500 ms Inventory latency. Expect roughly +1500 ms customer latency before mitigation. Use a 400 ms timeout and unconfirmed-stock fallback, then repeat +1500 ms; the response should be faster but stock uncertain.
Check comparable time windows and the same route. Report request count, latency, success/failure, and fallback activity. Remove the fault and mitigation after the test.

fields.label: Experiment plan
fields.prompt: State route, dependency, fault, magnitude, expected blast radius, and abort condition.

fields.label: Steady state and hypothesis
fields.prompt: What did you measure before the fault, and what do you predict?

fields.label: Fault result
fields.prompt: Record your actual fault commands, time window, customer effect, and dependency signals.

fields.label: Mitigation and reason
fields.prompt: Which timeout/fallback settings did you change, and why?

fields.label: Identical-fault validation
fields.prompt: Reapply the same fault and compare route latency, success, and fallback behavior.

fields.label: Conclusion, trade-off, and rollback
fields.prompt: Did resilience improve? What risk remains? How did you restore the clean state?

overview.title: 4 · Your own experiment
overview.description: Choose one customer risk, reproduce it, and support a mitigation with your own measurements.
